title: Grace to a broken women part 2
scripture_text: ‘’Jesus went to the Mount of Olives. At dawn he appeared again in the temple courts, where all the people gathered around him, and he sat down to teach them. The teachers of the law and the Pharisees brought in a woman caught in adultery. They made her stand before the group and said to Jesus, “Teacher, this woman was caught in the act of adultery. In the Law, Moses commanded us to stone such women. Now what do you say?” They were using this question as a trap, in order to have a basis for accusing him. But Jesus bent down and started to write on the ground with his finger. When they kept on questioning him, he straightened up and said to them, “Let any one of you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her.” Again he stooped down and wrote on the ground. At this, those who heard began to go away one at a time, the older ones first, until only Jesus was left, with the woman still standing there. Jesus straightened up and asked her, “Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you?” “No one, sir,” she said. “Then neither do I condemn you,” Jesus declared. “Go now and leave your life of sin.”
devotional:
A problem text

If you look carefully at how this text is introduced, you will notice that it says something like: - ‘The most ancient Greek manuscripts do not include John 7:53-8:11.’

This may not seem too important, but there is a history behind the exclusion of this passage which helps us understand how the early church struggled with it.

When it comes this passage, there seems to be a bit of a mystery. Many of the early manuscripts and papyri include it, the earliest church fathers quote it as scripture, and it is written in the same style as the rest of John’s gospel. Why then did some copyists not include it? What’s going on here?

Writing about this passage in his book on the gospel of John, Leon Morris said, ‘‘Throughout the history of the church it has been held that, whoever wrote it, this little story is authentic. It rings true. It speaks to our condition. It is worth our while to study it, though not as an authentic part of John’s writing. The story is undoubtedly very ancient. Most authorities agree that it is referred to by Papias. It is mentioned also in the Apostolic Constitutions. But it is not mentioned very often in the early days. The reason probably is that in a day when the punishment for sexual sin was very severe among the Christians this story was thought to be too easily misinterpreted as countenancing un-chastity. When ecclesiastical discipline was somewhat relaxed the story was circulated more widely and with a greater measure of official sanction.’’ Leon Morris Gospel of John pp 883

It is likely that the early church struggled with this passage because they did not really or could not grasp the full nature of the message of grace. For example, the ‘Shepherd of Hermas’, writing in the early second century, held that Christians who committed serious sins could be forgiven once after public confession and penance. The amazing thing is that he was roundly criticized by his contemporaries…for being too lax! For example, Tertullian called him ‘the shepherd of adulterers.’ It's easy to see why legalistic people- especially men wouldn't like this passage.

The early church thought that what happened in this story would encourage sin, so they refused to teach it. This was based on a misunderstand of grace. They confused the showing of grace with condoning sin. We will never be able to live a holy life if we do not understand and accept grace, grace will never condone or encourage sin: Look at what Titus 2:11-12 says: -

‘For the grace of God that brings salvation has appeared to all men. It teaches us to say no to ungodliness and worldly passions and to live self-controlled, upright and godly lives in this present age.’

Basically these verses are saying that we cannot live self-controlled and holy lives unless we are being motivated by grace.
prayer: Father thank you that grace keep us from sinning.
